newsitem.title: CHINA: China gold industry offers poor profit prospects.
newsitem.headline: China gold industry offers poor profit prospects.

text.p: Poor prospects for turning a profit from gold mining in China are likely to deter foreign companies from investing in the industry, Chinese and Western officials said.

Limited investment returns, the need for huge investment, a low gold price, difficulties in reaching agreement on profit-sharing and the poor selection of projects open for foreign investment were among problems for potential foreign investors, they said in interviews this week.

The signing last weekend of China's first gold mining joint venture would not necessarily encourage other foreign companies to invest, an official of China's Gold Bureau, under the Ministry of Metallurgical Industry, said.
"The outlook is not optimistic," he told Reuters.
"Setting up a gold mining joint venture needs a big investment but offers a low profit," he said.

China's Zhaoyuan Gold Industrial Group and Canada's Asia Minerals Corp last weekend signed a $75 million, 50-50 deal to develop the Yinggezhuang mine in eastern Shandong province, aiming to expand production to two tonnes a year.
The joint venture still needed the approval of the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation, the Gold Bureau official said.
China opened low-grade gold mines to foreign partners on a trial basis in August 1993 and in May 1996 agreed to allow foreign firms to conduct risk protection in central and western China.
"It is difficult for foreign companies to earn money from low-grade gold mines," Sun Tiemin, vice president of Asia Minerals Corp, said in an interview.
"The selection of projects open to foreign companies is too small." Sun said, adding that China should further open its gold industry.
The Gold Bureau official said low gold prices were also a disincentive to foreign exploration firms.
China reported in January that the domestic gold purchase price had been cut by 5.0 yuan per gram to follow a slide in prices of the metal on the international market.
The Chinese government controls domestic prices, adding a 10 percent premium, and requiring all gold mined in China to be sold to the central bank.
Hong Kong bullion ended at $343.10 an ounce on Wednesday, against New York's $343.70/344.20 close on Tuesday.
Prices went as high as $400 an ounce in 1996.
Another difficulty foreign investors faced was a plethora of bureaucratic procedures requiring them to go through many different departments to set up their investment, Sun said.
"They treated us just like a traditional state-owned enterprise," he said, adding that the firm has been negotiating with China since 1993.
"If our contract cannot be approved, it will discourage other foreign companies," Sun said.
The Gold Bureau official said several other projects have been considered but he declined to give details.
"We are still groping our way," he said.
China produced 35 tonnes of gold in the first four months of this year, which accounted for 35 percent of the target for the whole of 1997 and was an increase of 20 percent over the year-ago period.
